## Session outcome

Predict a two-phase state, solve it, then check both component balances.

**Before class:** Review chemical potential, fugacity and activity standards in Modules 2–3.

[Learning path and all labs](labs/learning-path.html#session-1)

::: {.notes}
This sequence uses the existing pre-midterm Modules 1–3 as prerequisites. Use questions to identify missing concepts rather than repeating the full reference decks.
:::

## The 180-minute class

| In class | Minutes |
|---|---:|
| Recall and prediction | 10 |
| Concepts and derivation | 45 |
| Worked example | 30 |
| Break | 10 |
| Instructor lab demonstration | 25 |
| Guided student exploration | 35 |
| Discussion and interpretation | 15 |
| Exit question and independent task | 10 |

::: {.notes}
Includes a 10-minute break. The 60 minutes of demonstration and guided work are part of the 180 minutes. If discussion runs long, move the optional extension to independent practice; do not remove the balance/interpretation check.
:::

## The equilibrium problem

At fixed temperature and pressure, a stable equilibrium minimizes total Gibbs energy subject to material conservation.

$$\mu_i^L=\mu_i^V\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \hat f_i^L=\hat f_i^V$$

A calculation also needs a phase model, composition constraints and a stability check.

::: {.notes}
Recall Modules 2–3 rather than reteaching EOS history. Ask which equality a mass balance cannot establish.
:::

## Liquid and vapor descriptions

$$y_i\hat\phi_i P=x_i\gamma_i P_i^{sat}\phi_i^{sat}\Pi_i$$

- Ideal vapor, ideal liquid: all correction factors are one.
- Modified Raoult: retain liquid activity coefficients.
- Gamma–phi: also retain vapor and reference-state corrections.

Lab 01 uses ideal vapor. Lab 09 adds second-virial vapor corrections.

::: {.notes}
Explain pure-liquid standard state and saturation reference. Phi–phi with PR/SRK remains reference-deck theory; it is not a supported lab option.
:::

## Four boundary calculations

| Specified | Unknown boundary | Composition supplied |
|---|---|---|
| T | Bubble P | Liquid x |
| T | Dew P | Vapor y |
| P | Bubble T | Liquid x |
| P | Dew T | Vapor y |

A dew calculation generally needs an inner liquid-composition iteration because γ depends on x.

::: {.notes}
Have students identify degrees of freedom before choosing a calculator panel.
:::

## Ideal-mixture boundary equations

$$P_{bubble}=\sum_i x_iP_i^{sat}$$
$$\frac{1}{P_{dew}}=\sum_i\frac{y_i}{P_i^{sat}}$$

Both equations are for fixed T, ideal liquid and ideal vapor. Using the same numerical composition in each equation describes different incipient-phase states.

::: {.notes}
Derive by substituting y_i=x_i Psat_i/P and applying normalization. Do not carry these closed forms unchanged into composition-dependent gamma.
:::

## TP flash includes a material balance

$$z_i=(1-\beta)x_i+\beta y_i,\qquad y_i=K_i x_i$$
$$\sum_i\frac{z_i(K_i-1)}{1+\beta(K_i-1)}=0$$

Here β is vapor mole fraction. In a nonideal liquid, K depends on the unknown x, so composition and phase fraction must be solved together.

::: {.notes}
Derive Rachford–Rice by eliminating x and y. Emphasize β in [0,1], single-phase checks and convergence of the outer iteration.
:::

## A reproducible ideal baseline

Lab 01 synthetic binary at 350 K: $P_1^{sat}=150$ kPa and $P_2^{sat}=60$ kPa. Choose ideal liquid, $z_1=0.5$, $P=95$ kPa.

| Quantity | Expected result |
|---|---:|
| Bubble P at x₁=0.5 | 105 kPa |
| Dew P at y₁=0.5 | 85.7143 kPa |
| Flash x₁, y₁ | 0.388889, 0.614035 |
| Vapor fraction β | 0.493506 |

The values are synthetic definitions, not real-fluid measurements.

::: {.notes}
Allocate the worked-example block here and on the next slide. Let pairs calculate before revealing the full table. Verify using Lab 01 ideal mode, not default nonideal settings.
:::

## A check independent of the solver

$$0.5=(1-0.493506)(0.388889)+(0.493506)(0.614035)$$

The rounded result closes the component-1 balance. Component 2 must close as well.

Also check $x_1+x_2=y_1+y_2=1$ and equality of component fugacities. A small balance residual alone does not validate the physical model.

::: {.notes}
Have students recompute from displayed values and discuss rounding. Pressure between ideal dew and bubble bounds establishes the two-phase regime in this example.
:::

## Activity models change the liquid

One-parameter Margules, two-parameter Margules and NRTL share the same equilibrium criterion but predict different γ(x).

Hold the synthetic component properties and T fixed. Change only the liquid model or one interaction parameter.

A nonconvex liquid needs an LLE/VLLE stability analysis; it cannot simply be accepted as a stable VLE flash.

::: {.notes}
Use the model restrictions as a conceptual link to Session 3. Do not interpret a synthetic parameter change as measured mixture data.
:::

## Vapor corrections need a reference

$$\ln\hat\phi_i=\frac{P}{RT}\left(2\sum_j y_j B_{ij}-B_{mix}\right)$$
$$B_{mix}=\sum_i\sum_j y_i y_j B_{ij}$$

Lab 09 also evaluates pure saturated-vapor φ consistently. With all Bᵢⱼ=0, the ideal-vapor limit must be recovered.

::: {.notes}
Source: Lab 09 implementation and its linked DeVoe gas-mixture reference. Coefficients are volume per mole. A small Z−1 can hide cancellation and is not an accuracy guarantee.
:::

## A model comparison has controlled inputs

Compare the same T, P, feed and liquid model. Change only the vapor description first.

Record differences in boundary pressures, phase compositions and β. Then examine the declared B(T) range and the truncation guard.

PR/SRK, dense vapor and virial adiabatic flash are outside these lab solvers.

::: {.notes}
Separate numerical support from broader thermodynamic theory. The reference VLE/EOS decks contain extensions students can read later.
:::

## Class demonstration · Labs 01 and 09

[Open Lab 01](labs/?system=synthetic&model=ideal&T=350&P=95&z=0.5#experiment) · [Open Lab 09](labs/virial.html#vr-experiment)

1. Reproduce the ideal baseline and save its results.
2. Cross a phase boundary by changing pressure.
3. In Lab 09, first use zero Bᵢⱼ, then change only B₁₂.

Before each run, predict the direction of change.

::: {.notes}
25 minutes: 10 baseline, 5 boundary crossing, 10 vapor comparison. Explain that Lab 09 has its own synthetic property input and does not automatically inherit Lab 01 state.
:::

## Guided exploration · 35 minutes

In pairs, choose one baseline state and one controlled change.

- One student predicts; the other records units and model settings.
- Recalculate and independently check a component balance.
- Exchange roles and explain any unexpected result.

Use the guided worksheet in the lab and save the calculator export separately.

::: {.notes}
Circulate for 20 minutes, then invite two contrasting cases. Students should distinguish a solver rejection from evidence of physical impossibility.
:::

## Adiabatic flash as an extension

$$H_{feed}=(1-\beta)H^L(T,x)+\beta H^V(T,y)$$

At specified pressure and feed enthalpy, T is another unknown. A TP flash at the feed temperature does not impose this energy balance.

[Lab 07](labs/adiabatic.html#af-experiment) uses synthetic caloric data. Independent practice only if the core TP calculation is secure.

::: {.notes}
Do not attempt a second full demonstration. Assign as optional extension and require an energy residual, not only a phase split.
:::

## Exit question

Two calculations have the same T and P. One returns a bubble-point vapor composition; the other returns a flash vapor fraction.

What additional information distinguishes these problems?

What evidence would make a converged flash result unsuitable for use?

::: {.notes}
Expected: bubble uses specified liquid composition and incipient vapor; flash needs overall feed and amounts; inappropriate physical model, stability, range or source issues remain after numerical convergence.
:::

Retain the calculator export, your worksheet, a comparison plot/table and one independent check. State an assumption that limits your conclusion.
